newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Republicans meet again as Gingrich vote nears.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Republicans meet again as Gingrich vote nears.

text.p: House Republicans, fighting to shore up support for Speaker Newt Gingrich in face of his admitted ethics violations, held a closed-door meeting on Tuesday hours before the House vote on his re-election.

At least five Republicans have publicly announced they will not back Gingrich in the vote, scheduled for Tuesday afternoon shortly after the House of Representatives convenes at the start of the 105th Congress. Others remain undecided.
The new meeting, which leaders said had been scheduled for some time, followed a long session on Monday night at which Republicans discussed the ethics charges and Gingrich answered questions.
Gingrich and other Republicans predict he will win re-election -- the first Republican speaker to do so in successive congresses in 68 years.
Asked how he thought the vote would go when he arrived for Tuesday's meeting, a smiling Gingrich told reporters: "I think we'll be fine."
Representative Matt Salmon of Arizona, who had earlier said that Gingrich should step down, predicted he would be re-elected.
"I believe that he will be re-elected today," he told reporters going into the caucus. "I don't think there's a significant amount of movement to unseat the speaker."
Salmon added, however, that he had no choice but to vote for Gingrich on Tuesday.

House Banking Committee Chairman James Leach of Iowa became the most prominent Republican to defect Monday, saying that "the most responsible course of action for the speaker is to step down and for the members to choose another leader for the House."
Representative Mark Neumann of Wisconsin, announced that he would vote for Republican Leader Dick Armey as Speaker and Representative Linda Smith of Washington said she might vote for Leach.
Other defectors are Reps. Michael Forbes of New York and Tom Campbell of California.
If only 10 Republicans vote for other members as speaker, Gingrich could emerge without a majority, meaning that further ballots would be required.

Ohio Republican Representative John Boehner, chairman of the House Republican Conference, told reporters Monday night: "I really do expect tomorrow that there will be no question that Newt Gingrich will be the first Republican speaker re-elected in 68 years."

Boehner said Gingrich would win on the first ballot. But he said party leaders would continue to seek out undecided members to try to nail down their votes and that the party would meet again on Tuesday in advance of the election.

Gingrich has admitted that he brought discredit to the House by not doing enough to prevent the use of tax-exempt donations in a partisan political activity -- a college course he taught -- and by misleading ethics committee investigators looking into the matter.

The committee begins work on Wednesday on the punishment phase of the investigation and is widely predicted to recommend that the House vote on a reprimand, the third-severest penalty, later this month.
